Standby is a waitlist that lives in your calendar. Every seat is a calendar invite, and the attendee's own Yes or No decides who gets it. It is all serverless: Step Functions, SES, Lambda and DynamoDB.

I ran the Well-Architected Review skill from the Agent Toolkit in Claude Code, on the whole repository. It checked all two hundred sixty-one best practices of the live framework, and raised H2, a High reliability finding: seats can stay empty while people wait.

Standby can never give a seat to two people. A DynamoDB transaction makes sure of that. But it could give a seat to nobody. When a hold expires, the release step frees the seat, sends the cancellation, then offers the seat to the next person. If the email fails, Step Functions retries the step. The retry finds the seat already free and stops. Nobody is invited.

A natural run on the live stack did not reproduce it. The account's Lambda concurrency limit of ten spread the emails out and hid the bug, so I injected the fault on purpose. Thirty people, ten seats, nobody answers, and a temporary permission block that makes the cancellation email fail. In three of three trials, all ten seats stayed empty while twenty people waited. And every execution reported success, so an alarm on failures would never have fired.

The fix is one rule. Offer the seat first, then send the email, and do both again on every retry. Throttled emails are retried instead of giving the seat away, and a small reconciler repairs anything a failed step leaves behind.

Same fault, fixed code. Zero empty seats, in three of three trials. All thirty people were offered a seat. The cancellations still can't be sent, so those executions now fail, visibly. The seat matters more than the courtesy email.

Then I ran the review again on the fixed code. Both H2 best practices went from High to Implemented, and implemented best practices rose from fifty-four to fifty-nine. It also found something new: a cancellation that keeps failing is never sent again. That is next, with alarms. Standby never gave a seat to two people. Now it never gives a seat to nobody.
